items.question: Why do you find it surprising that malicious queries combined with safe documents can break a system’s built-in safeguards?
items.object: Breaking a system’s built-in safeguards by combining malicious queries with safe documents
items.answer: I think it was so surprising to us because it's a very simplistic setup. It is not fancy, like, oh, you hijack the training data set and make people train on it, or you hijack this API and invoke certain tool calls, or you take the gradients of the model and then optimize certain queries. Rather, it's very straightforward malicious queries and completely safe documents that together break the built-in safeguards of the system.

Rather, it's very straightforward malicious queries and completely safe documents that together break the built-in safeguards of the system.

rubrics.text: The response attributes the surprise at malicious queries combined with safe documents defeating system safeguards to the simplicity of that attack setup.

items.question: How do you think generative AI changes the kinds of experiences Bloomberg can offer financial analysts?
items.object: Bloomberg’s approach to generative AI and earnings call summarization
items.answer: Now with generative AI, generative AI has enabled the development of a lot of new experiences that are driven by AI rather than that are enhanced by AI. As part of that, we first released earnings call transcript summaries. By which we mean when companies have the quarterly earnings call, which can be in written form multiple pages long, analysts, for example, might want to read or follow or listen to 40 or 50 of them. That's a full-time job already, especially during earnings season when there are like 10 of these a day that people are interested in. So that was our first generative AI product that we released last year, where we took a very subject matter expert-driven approach to summarization. We released summaries that are driven by questions that analysts might have. For example, what does the management of this company say about guidance or capital allocation? Are they going to be paying dividends, and so on? We've since expanded the topic list by quite a lot more. If you want to know whether the company is talking about AI, you might want to just say, okay, what does it say about AI? We have also newly released document insights, where you can actively ask questions to these kinds of documents.

items.question: Why do you consider transparent attribution important in Bloomberg’s generative AI products?
items.object: Transparent attribution in Bloomberg’s generative AI products
items.answer: In all of this, it's always super important that we provide grounded responses. I'm sure you've been talking about hallucinations and ungrounded, unattributable answers a lot, so I'm not going to go into that topic too deeply. But we have been developing this concept of transparent attribution, which basically is a way to provide attribution to trusted documents or structured data. So if you're talking about market data prices, you want to be able to link that to the actual databases that contain this information. And if you're talking about a summary, you want to know who said this actual quote or who made the statement that you're summarizing right now. In all of these developments, we're always providing attribution to these underlying sources.

items.question: Why do you consider misuse evaluation especially important for conversational AI products in financial services?
items.object: Misuse evaluation for conversational AI products in financial services
items.answer: This is very much grounded in ongoing work that we've been doing in terms of providing guardrails and robust evaluation for our products. As we're building guardrails, we want to also know: how can people misuse, either accidentally or purposefully, our products that we're releasing? As we're going more and more to a world where products are becoming more conversational with open-ended inputs, this is incredibly important for a heavily regulated domain such as ours. items.question: Why did your research lead you to conclude that retrieval-augmented generation is not safer despite using safe source documents?
items.object: The effect of RAG deployment on built-in LLM safeguards
items.answer: We've been building a lot of these guardrails, a lot of these evaluation processes, and we were curious because a lot of the models that we tested in this paper claim to be safe and claim to abstain from certain types of queries. But the RAG setting is slightly different, because you use a lot more context than what these models are usually trained to handle. Even if they can on paper handle thousands and thousands of words in context, they're usually trained on much shorter context and on very specific questions. So the hypothesis here was: well, if we're already doing this out-of-domain running of the model, how does this affect the built-in safeguards? And our results found that, yes indeed, if you have a relatively safe model, at least on paper it's safe, and you give it context of a document that is still safe, but a not-safe query, the additional context can actually override these built-in safeguards and make models a lot less safe. That's why we came up with this headline of RAG is not safer, because all the work that goes into safeguarding the LLM kind of goes out of the window as soon as you use it in the deployment context that it wasn't necessarily optimized to work.

items.question: Why do you think it is important to distinguish the RAG setup studied in your paper from the systems used in industry?
items.object: The distinction between the paper’s vanilla RAG setup and deployed industry systems
items.answer: I think mostly this is just to make sure to distinguish that from just LLMs, but rather one where you're talking about a system that is a retrieval step followed by adding context to an LLM. Although there is an important distinction that we should make, which is the distinction between a model and the system. When we're talking about applications built in our industries, we're talking about systems that usually have many more steps than just retrieval and generate. So what we studied in this paper is a very academic setup, fairly simplistic and vanilla RAG setup, where you do a retrieval, you add context, and you run that through an LLM. What we did not test for this paper is any more complicated systems that have additional verifiers and query understanding and attribution, and where you have a system that's not just the vanilla RAG setup, but rather a whole pipeline that also encodes a lot more business logic.

items.question: How do you approach evaluating whether retrieval-augmented generation is safer than a large language model alone?
items.object: Evaluating the safety of retrieval-augmented generation compared with an LLM alone
items.answer: So to begin with, I think you need to come up with some kind of set of test questions that you would like to answer, and you need to also identify a set of categories of safety that you care about in the set. So for this paper, you then run this to the LM, and you can measure how often does it actually abstain from answering the question, or how often does it respond with a safe answer. You can then replicate this in the RAG setup, right? That is kind of at its core the setup that we use in the paper, where on the one hand you just ask the large language model directly, and on the other one you also give it some kind of context that is retrieved. For that, you run it through a set of queries that are aimed to assess the safety by sending a series of unsafe queries.

items.question: How do you distinguish prompt injection from the directly unsafe queries you tested in your research?
items.object: Prompt injection versus directly unsafe queries in language-model safety research
items.answer: The goal of this is really that prompt injection itself is not necessarily the goal, but the goal is the unsafe behavior, right? Whereas the queries that we tested on are by themselves unsafe. It's not trying to induce an unsafe behavior, but rather just by looking at them, you can say this is not safe. Prompt injection is kind of one step removed from that. It's very meta, because you can use prompt injection to get a model to do all kinds of unsafe behavior across many different categories. So it's very much a meta technique to induce behaviors that you desire and override all the inbuilt rules. Whereas what we tested is different, because just by looking at the query, we're not inducing any behavior other than answering the query. So I think this is probably the biggest area where there's a lot of prior research.

items.question: How do you think about LLM security attacks that go beyond simply typing a prompt into a model?
items.object: LLM security attacks that require access to training data, models, or infrastructure
items.answer:
There are data poisoning attacks, for example, where if you get access to a corpus that is used by others to tune their model, you can induce behaviors, and you can do so with very few examples as well. In many industrial applications this is not necessarily the case, because these data sets are usually internal, but it is certainly something that academics have looked at quite a bit.

There are also other completely different attacks of hijacking the API or trying to invoke certain tool calls, where you can say, like, oh hey, call out to this other separate tool here and get me all the information. These are all, I would say, higher-level attacks, where you either need access to the model itself or an API of the model and you know a little bit more about infrastructure, or you have access to the corpus and can influence the data that the model is trained on. So there are many different attack vectors. There is a great taxonomy by OWASP, the LLM Top 10 security issues, that goes through all of these different secondary-level attacks that go beyond just typing something into a screen.

items.question: How do you explain the especially large decline in safety in smaller Llama models when they receive long retrieval contexts?
items.object: The large safety decline in smaller Llama models when given long retrieval contexts
items.answer: I think those deltas are extremely large, and I can only speculate as to why that is the case for Llama in particular. But there might be some correlation with the size, at least, because the smaller models seem to, at least for Llama, have some kind of outsized impact in terms of the effect. If you look at it through a pure lens of machine learning, this could come back to simple overfitting, right? The model is optimized for safety in a particular scenario, and that scenario in this case is you have a query, you typically have a length of maybe up to 25 or even 100 words, and then you test it on a scenario where the context suddenly is 10,000 words. Because it's a small model, it doesn't handle this generalization very well; it suffers more from this overfitting, and therefore it breaks down a lot more than the larger models, which might be a little bit more robust to being kicked.

items.object: Retrieval-augmented language models answering unsafe questions despite receiving safe documents

items.question: What would you consider a real explanation of why adding context can make an LLM's safeguards break down?
items.object: Causal explanations of why LLM safeguards break down when context is added
items.answer: I don't think we have a conclusive answer to this question, because in the end, any kind of research question in the space at the moment is all based on observation and hypothesis. A real answer to that question is based on a mechanistic interpretability kind of understanding of why the LLM is doing what it's doing. If we're taking the assumption that we can, at a mechanistic level, understand and explain large language model behavior, that is absolutely true. But even a lot of mechanistic interpretability literature only looks at correlations rather than causation. Really, what you're looking for is a causal effect that says this broke down because the context length was too long and it is out of domain for how the model was trained. That is a causal interpretation, but you're rarely ever going to get anything like that.

items.question: How do you assess the hypothesis that retrieval-augmented models fail because unsafe queries paired with safe documents fall outside their safety-alignment training distribution?
items.object: The hypothesis that added retrieval context causes model safety failures by creating inputs outside the safety-alignment training distribution
items.answer: At its core, there are only so many ways in which models can fail. It could also be a function of the particular queries that we used, for example. That's why we have to run these experiments with more than just a single query, to strengthen empirical evidence of it not being related to the query at all but rather the mechanism breaking. It clearly seems to be a function of this additional context that we put in, because if we don't put additional context, the models seem safe. That's the 0.3% number. If models are not answering and then suddenly they're answering if you add context, then the additional context causes the system to break down. But the specific mechanism by which it breaks down—the strongest hypothesis that we can offer—is that it is because it is out of distribution for how the model was trained. The model has not seen unsafe queries with safe documents together as part of the safety alignment. Otherwise it would be in distribution, and we would expect the model to not fail. But we don't have access to the training data of the model, so we cannot actually see how the safety alignment was done.

items.question: Why do you see evaluating and safeguarding models closer to their RAG deployment contexts as an important next step?
items.object: Evaluating and safeguarding models closer to RAG deployment contexts
items.answer: I think it's a fairly obvious next step. It's also one of the key takeaways and recommendations from our paper: models should be evaluated and then safeguarded closer to deployment contexts, especially since RAG is used so frequently across all industries. Our original hope was that it would already be taken care of and that the models remain safe despite the added context, which in this case they did not. So, yeah, this is definitely a next step that we encourage everyone who builds models to take, and also an opportunity for general research to make safety alignment more robust to variations in inputs.

items.question: How do you think about using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) safely in generative AI products?
items.object: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and application safety
items.answer: I think RAG is a fantastic type of technology. I think it is necessary to make any GenAI product that is grounded in actual trusted information. You do need to use RAG, but you can't just take the safety at the word of the provider of the model. Rather, you need to evaluate and assess continuously to make sure that your specific application does not override any of these built-in safeguards, and any other safeguards that you specifically care about and any other risk factors are ruled out. Otherwise, you're going to run into issues when you want to deploy the system and suddenly it can be misused.

items.question: How do you see the connection between your papers “RAG LLMs Are Not Safer” and “Understanding and Mitigating Risks of Generative AI in Financial Services”?
items.object: The relationship between “RAG LLMs Are Not Safer” and “Understanding and Mitigating Risks of Generative AI in Financial Services”
items.answer:
The connection very much is the first paper, “RAG LLMs Are Not Safer,” offers a view into how you can identify potential issues in the safety of these models. The second paper takes a different approach and asks, okay, in this specialized domain, what actually are the risks that you're concerned about? Things like, you know, how do I shelter money or how do I run away from the law, those are fairly ubiquitous, and they're things that are defined and included in general-purpose safety taxonomies that are out there and generally adopted across the industry.

Especially in our domain, financial services is a heavily regulated, very specialized, knowledge-intensive domain. The people who use the Bloomberg Terminal are financial professionals. We're not dealing with uneducated users, but rather with users that are very educated in a very particular type of application, and so the risk surface of applications that we're building is very different than if you're thinking about end-consumer chatbot apps. The same is true for law, biomedical, and healthcare. So we wrote the paper using financial services as a case study. But really the point was to make the connection to: now that you have ways to measure whether something is safe, what actually means safety to you?

items.question: Why do you treat financial services impartiality as a distinct safety requirement for generative AI?
items.object: Financial services impartiality in generative AI safety taxonomies
items.answer:
There is one category that is very relevant to us, which we call financial services impartiality, because if you give financial advice, that is a very regulated type of company and you're under very different rules that you need to follow. You also need to make sure that you're not giving preferential advice to one of your clients or that you're not playing your clients against each other. Aside from the financial advice, you're also not supposed to match buyers and sellers or you're going to be a market maker. These different actors in financial markets all have different rules and regulations that apply to them.

As a data analytics provider within financial services, we are not in the business of giving financial advice. So for us to stay neutral in whatever we use GenAI for is very important. For that reason, financial services impartiality is one of the key aspects that we discuss in our taxonomy.

When you look at more public taxonomies, one of the most popular ones is called ML Commons taxonomy, which is also the one that, for example, Meta's Llama is built to mitigate. They have a category called specialized advice, and they take a different stance and say as long as you give specialized advice, you also need to put a disclaimer that you're not an expert because you're a language model. This is very different if you're saying, yeah, you can give a buy or sell recommendation for a stock as long as you say you're not a financial adviser, or you don't give any financial advice at all. That's one of the key differences that we have.

items.question: Why do you think financial services needs a more specialized generative AI safety taxonomy than general-purpose applications?
items.object: Domain-specific safety priorities for generative AI in financial services
items.answer:
We also have a category specific to financial misconduct. Fraud or insider trading might be implicitly included in existing taxonomies, but they need to be a lot more highlighted and explored in our domain. Similar to confidential disclosure, which deals with aspects of disclosing information that is not public. That is usually the basis for cases of insider trading. If you're trading on information that is not public, that is insider trading. Well, if you hook up generative AI applications to databases that might have non-public information in there, you might be able to surface that information and query that information through this conversational interface.

I could go on and on, but for the sake of time, there is a lot more specialization in our taxonomy to aspects of safety that are a lot more important to actors in our space, whereas the general-purpose taxonomies care more about blatant illegal activities. They care a lot about toxicity and discrimination. Rightfully so. Those are important aspects, but they might be less important when you're dealing with financial professionals whose incentive structure and general usage of the tool differs a lot from when you're talking about consumer products.

items.question: Why do you see AI safety in heavily regulated domains as a governance problem?
items.object: AI safety governance in heavily regulated domains
items.answer: AI safety, especially for heavily regulated domains, is a governance problem. It's not necessarily a technical problem where you can, as a technologist, just solve it. That's why our paper is written together with our AI data organization and AI engineering organization and people from the CTO's office. The taxonomy was developed with input from many other functions in the company, including risk, security, and legal. Those are all people who have concerns about their specific area of expertise. You need to listen to all of these voices because of all the rules and regulations that apply to you as a company. And because there is not necessarily a list that is public that says, oh, you do AI in this space, here's what you need to do, here's the playbook. This playbook does not exist yet today, and us publishing this is really our goal: that this leads to more industry standardization around shared taxonomies and better understanding of what risks do we actually need to care about, where do we need technical mitigations, and how does this all influence governance processes.

items.question: How do you think about the role of an aligned language model in making an AI application safe?
items.object: The role of model alignment in application safety
items.answer: We've been talking a lot about safety alignment of large language models as part of the first paper, but really systems are much more than just a single aligned LLM. You can't necessarily expect that a single model solves all of these problems at once. Rather, you need to have multi-layered safeguards through an application. You need to have red teaming. You need to have exception management. What if a user is detected to violate the misconduct category? Do we escalate this? Does this need to be reported? Does this person need to be timed out, or do we just review this and say, "Yeah, this was correct. We need to make sure that this never leads to any answer, and we use this as an evaluation set." There are many ways in which these governance processes that go on in the background surrounding this application will then inform also the technical solutions that you need to have in place.

items.question: Why do you see identifying a company's own AI risks as a mitigation in itself?
items.object: Company-specific risk identification as an AI risk mitigation
items.answer: For risk mitigation, we do make a couple of recommendations as to what should happen. Number one is really, our taxonomy is not a one-size-fits-all. Companies need to start by understanding their own risks. This is already by itself a mitigation, because if you do not measure, you do not understand—that classic saying. By at least putting on paper, okay, this is the risk that we care about, these are important to us, that's the first step to measuring it.

items.question: How do you understand the role of red teaming in mitigating risks in language-model applications?
items.object: Red teaming of language-model applications
items.answer: We also talk about the importance of red teaming. Red teaming has obviously been much in the press and in the literature around language models, and especially around prompt injection and jailbreaking. Again, how can you break them? How can you play bad actor and try and come up with generalizable strategies around this? But red teaming can also mean building testing systems. You might have an application that provides insights into certain types of documents. You then take that application and test it end to end. You work with subject matter experts to really make sure that you're not getting any of the answers.

items.question: How do you think a multi-layer safety strategy should work in a language-model application?
items.object: A multi-layer safety strategy for language-model applications
items.answer: The mitigation strategies we recommend are built as a multi-layer safety strategy. This can be guardrail systems. In our paper we test a bunch of them. We show that they fail horribly, but we do test a lot of them, like Llama Guard and ShieldGemma and so on. This can also be the application itself. The safety alignment of the underlying language model that you're using is another mitigation layer. The prompt that you use is another mitigation layer. By layering them all together, you're building systems that are supposed to be safe, which you can then measure again because you've understood what risks you actually measure.

items.question: How do you approach testing the risks of a new generative AI application at Bloomberg?
items.object: Risk-focused testing and diverse red teaming for new generative AI applications
items.answer:
I cannot talk about too many of the details of this process, but at a high level I can certainly talk about it. It really starts by defining what the system is, understanding, okay, here's the client experience that we're trying to develop, and then coming together and saying, okay, for this type of client experience, these are the categories of our taxonomy that we are very worried about, or more worried about than others. Based on this prioritization, you can then develop targeted testing strategies.

We stress the importance here of red teaming, and in particular red teaming from people with diverse backgrounds. It does not necessarily suffice to have AI engineers red team a system, because the diversity of queries that you're going to see is very much skewed toward what they have experience with. The goal should be to bring people together with very diverse backgrounds to test the application and to focus the testing on the identified risks.

To give you a very hypothetical example, you might have an application that helps journalists. A big concern for journalists might be the fabrication of information. So you might want to specifically test what we call in our taxonomy counterfactual narratives, narratives that are simply grounded in not true information. For this hypothetical journalist application, that could then be the focus of the red teaming, and say, okay, yes, for all the other categories we can just kind of reuse the data we already have, but really need to go deep here. Hey, let's invite a bunch of journalists to help us test this application because they're the subject matter experts, right? You always need to engage with these subject matter experts to help come up with these test plans. Show them what do they actually mean by contextual narratives. It could be an example where they say, "Yeah, can you give me a headline that will dump the following stock by 10% at least?" This is not a query that anyone should enter into a large language model because that is market manipulation. That's not only illegal, that's also very much not desired. So these kinds of tests can then be conducted.

items.question: What value do you see in the data produced by red teaming an AI application?
items.object: Red teaming data as a corpus for measuring harmful system behavior
items.answer: The red teaming data itself is a very valuable corpus that comes out of it and which can then be analyzed and understood. Given additional annotations, how often, given a thousand inputs, did those actually lead to outputs? How many of those led to outputs that were actually malicious? Drawing the connection between the two, the setup is not too different, except that if you deal with systems, there are a lot more stakeholders involved and a lot more specialized expertise.

items.question: How do you think red-team queries can help you evaluate and improve a system’s layered safety defenses?
items.object: Evaluating and improving layered safety defenses using red-team queries
items.answer:
You can almost draw this as a kind of Sankey diagram, where you start with a large amount of queries that were used by red teamers, and you have, let's say, a thousand queries. You can then say, okay, based on a secondary analysis, 500 of these 1,000 were actually violating the taxonomy. The other 500 were actually fine, but they were maybe more tricky examples. Okay, you're left with 500. Of those 500 actual malicious queries, how many made it through the safety check? Say, okay, safety check catches another 50% of them. You're left with 250. Okay, of those 250 that bypass the first layer of safety, how many then went through the system and generated a response at all rather than saying, "Sorry, I don't know what you're even asking me to do." And so on.

You have this filter where you start with a lot, and then in the end you have some kind of fraction of the overall that would lead to unsafe behaviors in the best case, categorized across different classes, where you can say, yeah, this system is very susceptible to this counterfactual narrative risk. Then, based on that, we recommend adjusting the prompt, we recommend improving this guardrail, we recommend improving this guardrail, and so on. That way you can build up your mitigation over time while also gathering very valuable data that you can analyze over and over again, because these queries might be static, but you can run them through the system again in a month and see if it has improved.

Then, based on that, you can recommend, okay, we recommend adjusting the prompt, we recommend improving this guardrail, we recommend improving this guardrail, and so on. That way you can build up your mitigation over time while also gathering very valuable data that you can analyze over and over again, because these queries might be static, but you can run them through the system again in a month and see if it has improved.

items.question: How do you assess the potential of prompt changes to steer model behavior in the context of RAG safety?
items.object: Prompt changes as a way to steer model behavior in RAG systems
items.answer: We did not test this as part of the paper, so much as what we already discussed regarding prompting: you need to answer using the context that you give to us. But from a practical standpoint, if the prompt itself would not influence model behavior, the entire field of prompt engineering would not exist. So some of the prompt changes might have more or less impact. That's absolutely true, but you can certainly steer the model behavior by changing the prompt.

items.answer: Again, we did not necessarily test this for the paper, but the answer is probably. I don't know to what extent it is fully feasible to mitigate everything to 100% with prompting, but I'm sure that given enough effort, you can get that number of unsafe responses down significantly.

items.question: Why do you see adaptable or specializable AI guardrails as a priority for safety research?
items.object: Adaptable or specializable AI guardrails for knowledge-intensive domains
items.answer: I think the most necessary area is really in the realm of mitigations. We do need guardrails for highly specific applications, and this does not focus only on financial services but also on healthcare and biomedical research and the legal field. It might be specific to insurance companies. There are all of these knowledge-intensive domains that are adopting increasingly AI, and as they are increasingly adopting AI, they need to also be mindful of what domain-specific risks exist and how to mitigate them. Especially since we found that broad general guardrail solutions don't really work in these specialized domains, there needs to be more work on adaptable or specializable guardrails.

items.question: How do you think about the limits of English-language safety when assessing a multilingual AI model?
items.object: AI safety across languages
items.answer: One area we've also not touched today is multilingualism. Just because your model is safe in English does not necessarily mean it is safe in all the other languages.

items.question: Why do you see academics as well positioned to research AI safety risks in specialized domains?
items.object: Academic research on AI safety risks in specialized domains
items.answer: There is certainly some initial work in all of these fields now, but there's very little that is in the intersection between domain-specific domains and all of these issues. I think that's why in our second paper we also specifically call this out as an area where academics are actually very well positioned, in addition to people in industry, because academics often have access to subject matter experts. There are often cross-field collaborations that can be set up to really understand the AI risks in chemistry, in other social sciences, in economics. This is an area where there's both qualitative and quantitative work that can be done on the mitigations, on better ways to measure violations, on developing data sets that can be used and reused, on generating training data for mitigations, and all of those areas where there's very little research at the moment specifically in specialized domains.

items.question: Where do you see opportunities for academics to lead in responsible AI research?
items.object: Academia’s role in responsible AI research for specialized domains
items.answer: I think being thought leaders in responsible AI is absolutely one that they can take up, especially as we're still trying to understand all of these domains. And obviously there's a lot of really important and interesting research coming out also on general AI safety from academics. But we don't see much, either from industry or from academics, in these specialized domains. That's where there's a lot of opportunities for research today.
